accuracy.evidence: Matches NGSS K-PS3-1 and K-PS3-2 and their clarification that kindergarten compares relative warmth (warmer/cooler) rather than measured temperature, so the lab shows only cool, warm and hot. The physics is right: shade is blocked direct sunlight, shaded things still warm slightly from warm air, dark surfaces absorb more light, and water warms more slowly than sand.

misconceptions.evidence: Directly targets 'shade makes cold' (the shaded stone still warms a little and the text says shade only blocks sunlight), 'the sun only gives light', 'any roof keeps things cool' (clear plastic fails), and unfair comparisons: the lab refuses to run if both stones sit in one place or if a can sits in the shade during the colour test.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsun is a sun-and-shade yard with a drag-to-place basket, hour-by-hour warming bars and sunlight rays, a draggable sun on a day arc that warms and cools a slide, and a roof-testing rig over a dog's bowl. It differs from flagwarm (sorting hot and cold), flagmelt (ice melting) and flagtherm (reading a scale).

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step isolates one variable: sun versus shade with identical stones, dark versus white with both cans in the sun, sand versus water with equal sun, then time of day, then the engineering task in K-PS3-2 where children try roofs and see that only one that blocks light keeps the water cool.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions come before the evidence: which stone warms, which can warms, sand or water, when the slide is hottest, and whether a clear roof works. The clear-roof prediction is set to catch the 'any roof makes shade' idea, and each step's reveal line confirms or corrects the guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions each map wrong answers to a targeted reply from why(): 'Shade does not make cold. It only blocks the sunlight', 'Sunlight gives warmth as well as light', 'Clear plastic lets the sunlight through', 'A net lets lots of sunlight through its holes' and the fair-test reply for colour.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short concrete sentences about stones, T-shirts, sand, the sea and a slide, and pass the family kid FK gate. Adult paragraphs were cut into shorter sentences to pass the 10.0 gate while keeping the quoted standards, the physics and the named mistakes.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a fact, a cause or a method: what shade is, why dark and sand warm faster, when the ground peaks, and how to build a shade. The content gate found no banned phrases and low overlap with Hot, warm and cold and Melting and freezing.

mobile.evidence: On a 360 px Android screen in both themes the stones, cans, trays, warmth bars and level pills sit apart without overlap, roof cards show short names, and every drag has a full-width button (Stone 1 → sun, Wait 1 hour, Morning, Umbrella, Wait until midday).

accessibility.evidence: Each action writes a full sentence to the canvas aria-label and live region, such as which thing is cool, warm or hot at each hour. Level pills use dark fills (#1d4ed8, #b45309, #b91c1c) under white text. axe reported no violations on desktop and iPhone in light and dark themes.

sources: NGSS Lead States (2013) Next Generation Science Standards, K-PS3-1 'Make observations to determine the effect of sunlight on Earth's surface' and K-PS3-2 'Use tools and materials to design and build a structure that will reduce the warming effect of sunlight on an area', with clarification statements and assessment boundaries (relative measures only)
NGSS Disciplinary Core Idea PS3.B Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer: 'Sunlight warms Earth's surface' (grades K-2)
National Science Teaching Association, kindergarten energy storyline notes on student ideas that shade 'makes cold' and on fair comparison when testing surfaces
NASA Earth Observatory, 'Climate and Earth's Energy Budget': absorption by dark and light surfaces (albedo) and the higher heat capacity of water than of land
